walkthroughs.body_html: Shakespeare wrote Macbeth in 1606, soon after James I, a Scottish king, took the English throne. The play flatters him: Banquo (a supposed ancestor of James) is honourable; the witches' show of kings in Act 4 stretches to James himself. The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 also explains the play's fear of secret regicide.

Duncan is presented as a holy king whose 'virtues will plead like angels'. Macbeth's murder of him is therefore a cosmic offence. The play contrasts Macbeth's tyranny with Edward the Confessor's healing touch in Act 4 - a model of sacred kingship - and ends with Malcolm restoring the natural order.

Lady Macbeth dares her husband: 'When you durst do it, then you were a man.' She links manhood to murder. After Duncan's death, Macbeth himself adopts that logic - hiring murderers, slaughtering Macduff's family. Shakespeare exposes how a narrow definition of masculinity becomes a tool of evil.
